description: Hello, We are ViviTed gums. We are very happy to represent our great country Turkey and represent our school.
summary: Our project, aims to help humans explore and eventually survive on Mars. Our project combines an intelligent survival map and futuristic technology. While exploring around the Jezero crater, our tech will encourage us to research the human body activities on a planet with less gravity, no atmosphere and extreme temperatures. With this project we hope to plan a successful Mars walk and evaluate the opportunity to make many new inventions and gain more knowledge.
details:
Vivited is a web based Martian exploration and mission planning prototype built for Jezero crater. We wanted NASA’s surface data (imagery, elevation, weather, rover stations) to feel usable on one map, the way a crew might actually ask: can we walk there, what science is waiting, and do we still have enough to get home?

The question we kept in the centre of the project is:

How can astronauts explore Mars safely, check earlier robotic observations, and collect new scientific data using one interactive map?

The system has four main parts.

Interactive map of Jezero (Orbit, Map, and Terrain)

The frontend is a Flutter web app. You start from orbit, enter the site, and explore Jezero around 18.44°N, 77.45°E. The map uses the same kind of plate carrée framing as the USGS products, so the layers sit on the terrain instead of fighting it.

You can switch between CTX optical imagery and shaded relief, turn analysis layers on and off, and look at the same area in a 3D terrain view. The layers include slope hazard, THEMIS night infrared, solar exposure, shadows for the planned time of day, and a walk back time field to the airlock. Perseverance’s traverse is there too, as a quiet reminder that this ground has already been driven.

There is also a DEMO button that walks a judge through the live interface in a few minutes. No login, no setup maze.

Mission interface: habitat, checkpoints, and four routes

We did not want abstract pins with no story. So we placed five educational marks on real Perseverance stations.

H0 is a fictional habitat at Three Forks. The place is real; the habitat role is simulation. CP1 is the terrain checkpoint at Amalik. CP2 is the validation checkpoint at Wildcat Ridge. CP3 is the discovery checkpoint at Bright Angel / Cheyava Falls. SH is the safety and staging mark at Octavia E. Butler Landing.

If a coordinate is on the map, the rover was there. We did not invent locations.

Then we built four routes with different jobs inside the same study area.

Route A (Safe Access) goes from the habitat into the fan front area on manageable ground. Route B (Validation) checks early robotic geology on the crater floor. Route C (Discovery) goes out toward Cheyava Falls and a new scientific question. Route D (Return) is a corridor home to Habitat H0, tied to life support thinking.

We also kept a rim climb as a stress case, mostly so the go/no go checks have something they should refuse. These are educational planning corridors, not NASA approved walking paths.

In Plan you can load a route, move the airlock, add stops, change season and egress time, and watch distance, elevation change, slope, duration, and oxygen update. Rehearse plays the walk against the clock: where you are, oxygen left, walk back time, Sun, MEDA climatology, and a simple timeline of events.

Life support thinking you can actually follow

We have two layers here on purpose.

The planner uses published walking and metabolic models (Marquez for speed, Santee for energy, with Mars gravity) and editable suit assumptions. Routes are found with A* on the 20 m grid, with Dijkstra used when we want to double check ourselves. Steep ground can close a path. The app checks daylight, oxygen reserve, walk back, and other go/no go conditions.

Separately, there is a small educational simulator with transparent teaching units, because we wanted judges to see the arithmetic without pretending it is a flight suit. The sample case is the one from the educational brief: start with 100, walk 120 minutes at 0.3 per minute, keep a reserve of 20. You use 36, you have 64 left, reserve is fine. Stretch the mission and the app says, plainly: “Return to Habitat / Reduce Mission Time.” Same idea for battery. There is a banner that this is an educational simulation, not for real astronaut operations. We meant that.

Scientific data integration and honesty labels

Vivited bundles processed copies of public NASA / USGS products for Jezero: the Mars 2020 CTX stereo elevation model (20 m) and CTX orthomosaic, THEMIS night infrared, MOLA for the globe, Viking imagery for context, the Perseverance traverse and science stations, MEDA climatology (historical, not live weather), and MSL RAD dose as a simple radiation note.

Python scripts prepare those assets offline. The app itself runs in the browser from the bundled files, except optional Viking context tiles from NASA Trek when a connection is available.

We care a lot about not overselling the numbers. Throughout the interface we label things as NASA DATA for real measurements and imagery, SCIENTIFIC INTERPRETATION for things we derived (like hazard classes from slope), and SIMULATION for fictional habitat roles, teaching oxygen units, and planning assumptions.

If the data is missing, we show “no data.” We do not invent a wind speed to make the chart look complete. Sources is the page where every dataset, method, and limit lives, with links you can copy.

Technology Stack

Frontend / app: Flutter, Dart, Riverpod. Map and views: flutter_map, custom Orbit / Map / Terrain stages. Routing and science models: native Dart (A*, Dijkstra, Mars24 time, walking and metabolic models). Offline data prep: Python. Hosting: Firebase Hosting for the Flutter web build (build/web). No user authentication.

Scentific Data Sources

NASA/USGS Mars 2020 CTX DTM and orthomosaic. NASA Mars Trek (THEMIS, Viking). MGS MOLA. NASA/JPL Perseverance MMGIS waypoints and traverse. Mars 2020 MEDA (PDS Atmospheres). MSL RAD (Hassler et al. 2014).

Innovation Ideas

A lot of Mars viewers show beautiful images. What we tried to do is put imagery, topography, historical weather, route planning, and resource thinking in the same place, and keep the tone honest.

We want students and judges to feel the trade off: the science stop that looks exciting on the map may also be the one that burns your oxygen margin on the way home. Vivited is not a certified EVA planner and we do not claim NASA endorsement. Nobody has walked on Mars. A 20 m model cannot see every boulder. MEDA is climatology, not a forecast.

Still, we think there is value in a tool that makes those relationships visible. If someone opens Vivited and leaves understanding how NASA observations, terrain, science goals, and limited resources fit together, and where the models stop, then the project did its job.

If we continue, we would love finer obstacle data, dust scenarios, and multi crew timelines. Same rule as today: if we cannot source it, we do not fake it.
